lessons.title: Match Statements for Card Rules
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Match Statements

GDScript's `match` is a cleaner `switch`. It compares one expression against a series of patterns and runs the matching block. For Kadi's per-card rules, where each rank triggers different behaviour, `match` is the right tool.

```gdscript
func classify(card: CardData) -> String:
    match card.rank:
        CardTypes.Ranks.TWO, CardTypes.Ranks.THREE, CardTypes.Ranks.JOKER:
            return "penalty"
        CardTypes.Ranks.JACK:
            return "jump"
        CardTypes.Ranks.KING:
            return "kickback"
        CardTypes.Ranks.QUEEN, CardTypes.Ranks.EIGHT:
            return "question"
        CardTypes.Ranks.FOUR, CardTypes.Ranks.FIVE, CardTypes.Ranks.SIX, \
        CardTypes.Ranks.SEVEN, CardTypes.Ranks.NINE, CardTypes.Ranks.TEN, \
        CardTypes.Ranks.ACE:
            return "answer"
        _:
            return "normal"
```

Group multiple values on one line with commas. The `_` wildcard catches anything unmatched — always include it so unhandled ranks fail loudly instead of silently dropping.

`match` works on ints, Strings, enums, arrays, and dictionaries. It does NOT fall through — only the matched block runs.

> [!WHY]
> `match` lays every card rule out like a lookup table. Adding a new special card (say, a custom rank) is one new line — and the compiler does not need to re-evaluate every `if/elif` above it. Compared to a long if/elif chain, match makes the rule book visually parallel to the code, which is invaluable when a designer is reviewing the logic beside you.

Use `match` when one value selects among many discrete branches; use `if/elif` when each test is its own boolean expression.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write a `match` on `card.suit` returning the strings "red" for HEARTS/DIAMONDS and "black" for CLUBS/SPADES, with a `_` default returning "unknown".
practicePrompt.hint: Group the red suits on one line and the black on another.
practicePrompt.solutionCode:
func suit_color(card: CardData) -> String:
    match card.suit:
        CardTypes.Suits.HEARTS, CardTypes.Suits.DIAMONDS:
            return "red"
        CardTypes.Suits.CLUBS, CardTypes.Suits.SPADES:
            return "black"
        _:
            return "unknown"

quizQuestions.prompt: What does the `_` pattern in a match statement match?
quizQuestions.explanation: `_` is the wildcard; it matches anything and should be the last branch to catch unhandled cases loudly.

quizQuestions.prompt: Does a `match` branch fall through to the next branch if it has no return?
choices: No — only the matched block runs, there is no fall-through
quizQuestions.explanation: Godot's `match` does not fall through. Each branch is independent; you must explicitly `return` or fall out.

lessons.title: Drawing Cards and Handling Invalid Plays
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Drawing Cards and Handling Invalid Plays

Validation is only half of Kadi's play loop — the other half is what happens when a play does *not* go through. The rulebook is precise: if a player **cannot** play a card, they must draw one from the draw pile; if a player plays a card that does **not** match the suit or rank of the top card, they are penalised by picking a card from the draw pile and the game proceeds to the next player.

Both cases funnel through one function, `draw_card(player)`. It also handles the empty-pile rule: when the draw pile runs out, the discard pile — excluding its top card — is reshuffled to become the new draw pile.

```gdscript
func draw_card(player: int) -> CardData:
    if GameState.deck.is_empty():
        var top: CardData = GameState.discard_pile.pop_back()
        GameState.deck = GameState.discard_pile
        GameState.deck.shuffle()
        GameState.discard_pile = [top]
    var card: CardData = GameState.deck.pop_back()
    GameState.hands[player].append(card)
    return card
```

The player triggers a voluntary draw through a **Draw button** — a `Button` node whose `pressed` signal we connect in `_ready()`. Attempted plays route through `try_play`, which uses the `is_playable` validator from the previous lesson: a legal card moves to the discard pile, an illegal one costs the player a penalty draw and their turn.

```gdscript
@onready var draw_button: Button = $UI/DrawButton
@onready var feedback_label: Label = $UI/FeedbackLabel

func _ready() -> void:
    draw_button.pressed.connect(_on_draw_pressed)

func _on_draw_pressed() -> void:
    draw_card(TurnManager.current_player_index)
    feedback_label.text = "Card drawn — no playable card."
    TurnManager.advance_turn()

func try_play(player: int, card: CardData) -> void:
    if is_playable(card, GameState.discard_pile.back()):
        GameState.hands[player].erase(card)
        GameState.discard_pile.append(card)
    else:
        draw_card(player)
        feedback_label.text = "Invalid play! Penalty card drawn."
        TurnManager.advance_turn()
```

Notice that the invalid branch never crashes and never silently ignores the click. It applies the rulebook's penalty (one drawn card), tells the player exactly what happened through the `feedback_label`, and passes the turn — the same three beats a human dealer would perform at a real table.

> [!WHY]
> Invalid input is not an error condition in Kadi — it is a rule with a defined consequence. Coding the penalty path as deliberately as the happy path keeps the game fair and the player informed. A silent rejection teaches nothing; a crash ruins the match. UI feedback plus a rulebook-accurate penalty turns every mistake into a lesson about which cards match, which is exactly how people learn Kadi at a real table.

With drawing and penalties wired, the play loop is complete: match, play, or draw — and the turn always moves on.

quizQuestions.prompt: Per the Kadi rules, what happens when a player plays a card that matches neither the suit nor the rank of the top card?
choices: They draw a penalty card from the draw pile and the turn passes to the next player
They are eliminated from the game
quizQuestions.explanation: An invalid play is penalised with one drawn card, and the game proceeds to the next player — the try_play else-branch encodes exactly this rule.

quizQuestions.prompt: How do you react to a Button being clicked in Godot 4?
choices: Connect its `pressed` signal to a handler: `draw_button.pressed.connect(_on_draw_pressed)`
quizQuestions.explanation: Buttons emit the `pressed` signal when clicked; connecting a callback in _ready() is the idiomatic Godot 4 pattern.

debugChallenge.bugDescription: In Kadi an Ace is special: a player may play it even when it does not match the top card, because an Ace lets them declare a new suit (and can also be used to escape a penalty). This validation treats an Ace like an ordinary card, so a player holding only an off-suit Ace is wrongly stuck and the game stalls.
debugChallenge.explanation: The missing `or card.rank == CardTypes.Ranks.ACE` clause meant an Ace was rejected unless it happened to match the suit or rank. Adding the check restores the rule that an Ace (like a Joker) may be played regardless of the top card, after which the player declares the next suit.
